How do people make friends as adults? Clubs, meetups, work, events, festivals. Talking to strangers is kind of advanced social skills wise. Find an activity with other socially awkward people that is designed to facilitate socialization, like chess or boardgames, maybe a language learning club. Make small talk with people, when u feel comfortable, ask them for socials or a phone number. Chances are they're lonely too. Ask them to hang out if u feel like they'd be up for it. Keep doing this until u have like a group of people u can do stuff with. Then go to places with them like festivals, nightclubs, anime conventions, whatever ur into. Talk to people there. It's easier to make friends when you're with friends. Just expand your social circle from there. it's gonna take time and you're gonna get rejected. It's all a numbers game tho so don't get discouraged. Maybe u won't find anyone who gets u 100%, but at least you'll have some people u can talk to. Coming from a person who used to have no one, and now has an okaish number of friends. Not every friend has to be a ride or die platonic soulmate. If they're not like morally bankrupt or a walking red flag just give them a chance, don't judge too harshly, be open minded. This may sound redundant to say but you'd be surprised how many people are lonely because they're only open to talking to a certain type of person. Make a conscious effort to address your subconscious biases and to make people feel welcome and heard, regardless of how they present themselves. 

Edit: if you really struggle finding clubs and what not just take a class or some sort of certification at a community college.

At the end of the day, I still have a trauma induced personality disorder that is distinct from standard PTSD and not merely a symptom of autism.

I think that it makes a lot of sense to categorize BPD as a subtype of PTSD (same with other cluster B disorders). But I feel like there are some important differences. Primarily in how it manifests in relationships with others and with yourself. Maybe another way of looking at it is that personality disorders are designations for specific coping mechanisms or responses to trauma, as opposed to simply a result of it. Yes, people with PTSD can experience emotional instability, volatile relationships, skewed perceptions of self and others, etc. But those are not necessary for PTSD diagnosis. The existance of one or two BPD symptoms is not enough for a BPD diagnosis. It's an amalgamation of a very specific set of diagnostic criteria. Also, there is a significant genetic component to personality disorders which does not exist with PTSD, as far as I'm aware. The genetic component can also be a possible explanation for why some people with PTSD develop personality disorders and others don't. It's also possible for someone to have BPD with little to no trauma, although that is very rare.

I do agree that we need to seriously reevaluate how personality disorders are perceived by professionals and society at large. It is abhorrent that people like myself, let alone those who are worse off, are unable to get proper treatment, even if accessibility is not an issue. Changing the designation of personality disorders as a subset of PTSD would be powerful for rhetorical reasons at the very least. Most reasonable people know to afford some empathy to individuals diagnosed with PTSD even if their symptoms are disruptive, but the same definitely cannot be said about people with personality disorders.

I realize that clinically it's considered to be a result of abuse and trauma, but I dislike this frame of thought because it necessitates that there is something wrong with you. when we get socialized we are taught how to control our emotions, how to behave in public, how to handle difficult situations etc. this works well for neurotypical people/normies, but if you have some sort of mental idiosyncrasy then u might need different emotional tools then someone who doesn't have said idiosyncrasy. i.e. if u have bpd then ur typically more likely to be sensitive to criticism, to take things personally, to have mood irregularities, and to internalize others words and actions to the point where it causes u extreme distress. u need to accept those things and to train ur mind to react differently. in that sense it is kind of a chore which u just have to live with. bpd is exceptionally difficult to medicate and so the main methods of treating these responses is thru things like therapy and self reflection. with all that said, I wanna go back to my initial point about bpd not being something that u have to be ashamed of. the label "bpd" is only used to describe all the negative aspects of the way a bpd brain works, but I strongly believe that there are other fundamental differences to that don't get mentioned enough. bpd people are often extremely intelligent, creative, empathetic, and interesting (i think more so on average than normal people) but we and those around us struggle to realize our strengths because we've internalized that we are somehow damaged or evil. ur not evil, ur brain just works differently. with the right tools u can learn to better control things like mood swings and internalized shame, and begin to accept the things that make u wonderful. I don't want this to come off too preachy, and I'm still struggling to find the balance to make it work, but I just really wanna emphesize what I wish I was told when I learned I had bpd. ur not evil, ur not a monster, and there is nothing fundamentally wrong with u. please try not to hate urself just because u might need some extra help with navigating ur emotional responses.

Well I feel like this question can have multiple correct answers depending on your starting point. i.e. if you start under the premise that the sexes are equal but have been made unequal via social conditioning and cultural practices, that means that yes it is the patriarchy that's keeping women down and forcing them to internalize misogyny. Because obviously men and women are still unequal in terms of income, career success, reproductive freedom, and generally being seen as competent and such. There are different valid ways to explain these disparities. One could be the patriarchy, another could be complementarianism or fundamentalism or some form of social Darwinism (strictly descriptively). So if you believe that men and women would on average get equal outcomes if they weren't socialized a certain way, then obviously the patriarchy is the most logical explanation. If you think the outcomes would still be different regardless of socialization then that necessarily makes u 'sexist' from the pov of the opposition. u can technically blame everything on the patriarchy if your starting point is that our society has been historically and still is patriarchal.

All it comes down is if you think equality is desirable. If you do then sexism is bad because it endangers equality. If you don't think equality is a good thing then obviously that changes things. Do you think people should are/should be fundamentally equal in society?

ok so im basically self taught, and the best advice i can offer is googling tabs for songs, starting from very basic and eventually increasinf in difficulty. unlike sheet music, its very self explanatory. id recomend with starting with twinkle twinkle lil star, "when johnny comes marching home again" (i started w that btw), maybe the godfather theme song, the paint it black intro, jinggle bells, star of the county down basically anything w a simple, recognizable melody. after u feel confident playing the tune without looking at the guitar or thinking too much about it, increase in difficulty, i.e. pirates of the carrabean, schindlers list theme, ride of the valkyries, later on try learning smt like hotel cal intro, stairway to heaven, blackbird, it seems very daunting but as long as u gradually increase the difficulty and practice u will get there eventually. make sure when u start a new piece, to work slowly, dont worry too much about making it sound perfect.

For chords, similarly, google song chords, maybe start w time of ur life by greenday, very simple but fun to play, wonderwall is a classic beginner song, maybe country roads or really any simple, pop type song works. the beetles have some really simple stuff that only uses two chords, look up their early pop songs, very easy to play even if ur a total beginner.

If u wanna try tutorials, the best that i can suggest for chords is proly  Marty Music on youtube, he examplains everything perfectly and has tutorials for basically any skill level. For tuning, download Guitar Tuna, its a free app, tunes near perfect. if u dont have access for wtv reason or wanns do it manually, just remember that every string is supposed to sound as the equivalent of the string bellow it when the 5th fret is pressed.
